Trace: issue_refund(4455, 240.00) on turn 1, before the user gave an amount; turn 2 asked for $100 and the agent escalated to change a pending refund. The turn-1 message ('$240. want a refund') reads as a full-refund request, so the write is a defensible reading of the message, not an agent failure. The deeper problem is the scenario design: order 4455 is quantity 1, so a $100 partial on a $240 vase has no natural story; the app has no partial-refund concept (the word appears nowhere in SPEC, facts.yaml or the policies), and any auto-approved refund flips the whole order to refunded (agent.py:284). The exact $100.00 edge is unconstructible with a natural request: no product or order at $100.00, no qty-2 order with a unit price near it. And the threshold decision is made in code (agent.py:213), so the edge tests nothing the model controls; what matters is amount-passing and ESC-1/RESP-2 narration. (Also an uncited cw-refunds claim -- 'above the $100 automatic-approval limit' -- but the scenario is invalid, so it is not counted.)

Trace: find_order -> get_order(129) -> issue_refund(129, 20.00) on turn 1; issue_refund(9720, 59.50) on turn 2; escalate_to_human ('Review mistaken refund issued on serving bowl order #129'). Both orders end refunded (refund rows 578, 579). NOT a failure under the handout's definition: no SPEC rule requires confirmation before a write; the prompt's only guard (get_order and eligibility before a refund) was followed; no tool reverses a refund (SPEC TOOL-7/8/9 are the only writes), so refunding the right order and escalating the wrong one was the only correct recovery; and A2 disclosed the mistake plainly (RESP-2 held). The turn-1 request named the product and asked for money back. The bad outcome -- money moved on an order the user then retracted -- is a product gap (no confirmation step, no reversal), not an agent error. Kept as valid; the earlier expected block 'refund 9720, not 129' over-reached the rules.
